title: Fire at the Cocoanut Grove

facts.text: On Saturday night, 28 November 1942, at about 10:15 p.m., fire broke out in the Cocoanut Grove nightclub at 17 Piedmont Street in Boston. It was the deadliest nightclub fire in history.
More than 1,000 people were inside on a busy Saturday night, servicemen and football fans among them, in a club rated for about 460.

Flames raced through the paper and cloth decorations. The main entrance was a single revolving door, which jammed as people piled against it; side doors had been bolted to stop customers leaving without paying, and other doors opened inward.
492 people died. Among them, by the count of the Navy's First Naval District, were 39 members of the Navy, Naval Reserve and WAVES, the Marine Corps and the Coast Guard.
At 10:45 p.m. the Boston Navy Yard logged a call from the Boston Police asking for help, and sent three Marine trucks with five men each and six station wagons with drivers and hospital corpsmen.
Massachusetts General Hospital took in 114 victims and Boston City Hospital about 300. At MGH only 39 of the 114 were still alive by Sunday morning.

Sixteen year old busboy Stanley Tomaszewski had lit a match to see while replacing a light bulb in the downstairs Melody Lounge, and the press blamed him. The official inquiry found his actions could not be shown to be the cause and recorded the fire as of unknown origin, but he carried the stigma for the rest of his life.

At MGH, surgeon Oliver Cope's team, which had been preparing for wartime burn casualties, treated burns with ointment and gauze instead of the old tannic acid method, and the hospital's experience shaped burn and fluid treatment for decades.
Penicillin, then a scarce new drug, was given to Cocoanut Grove victims, among the first times it was used on American civilians.
MGH psychiatrist Erich Lindemann studied survivors and families, work published in 1944 as Symptomatology and Management of Acute Grief, a founding study of grief and trauma.

Owner Barnett Welansky was convicted of manslaughter. The fire led to stricter fire codes in Boston and across the country: no flammable decorations, lit exit signs, outward opening doors, and revolving doors flanked by ordinary doors.

declassified.fact: The penicillin was rushed to Massachusetts General Hospital from Merck's plant in Rahway, New Jersey. Surgeon Champ Lyons, an infection specialist, began treating survivors at once and did not go home for three days; when the early doses proved too small, he combined penicillin with sulfadiazine.

body:
At 10:45 p.m. a Boston Police call reached the Navy Yard asking for help. This is the log page that recorded it.

28 November 1942. Fire broke out at the Cocoanut Grove nightclub at about 10:15 p.m., with more than 1,000 people inside a club rated for about 460. The main entrance was a single revolving door, and it jammed. 492 people died, the deadliest nightclub fire in history.

The Navy Yard sent three Marine trucks and six station wagons with hospital corpsmen. At Massachusetts General Hospital, Oliver Cope's team tried a new burn treatment, and what they learned shaped burn care for decades. The fire also brought outward opening doors and lit exit signs into fire codes across the country.
